description: We are interested in data analysis, ML/AI, and math modelling, to solve important world challenges
summary:
In this research, we study how ocean data can predict water levels in advance and provide useful warning for coastal regions, using New York Harbor and Los Angeles as examples. We combine two complementary approaches.

First, using NASA and NOAA observations—tide gauges, climate indices, winds, pressure, and satellite sea-surface height—we show that ocean conditions outside a coastal region can improve local water-level prediction. We remove tides, model trends and seasonal cycles with least-squares and Fourier terms, then screen predictors and validate them on unseen winters. Tropical-Pacific El Niño conditions measured months earlier provide useful information about subsequent winter high-water risk on both U.S. coasts.

Second, we use ocean physics for fine-grained short-range prediction. NASA altimetry, GEOS-FP winds, and OSCAR surface currents feed a nonlinear shallow-water model. 

On 2023–2026 data, chronologically validated 14-day forecasts reduce sea-surface-height error by about 12% relative to persistence, with 92% of forecasts outperforming it.

Our interactive website presents both approaches through a 3D globe, East/West coast views, a “Test a winter” replay, charts, and live-updating NASA GIBS imagery, alongside results computed from records through October 2026.

Together, the project combines global Earth observations with data and physics-based ocean modelling to provide seasonal early warning and fine-grained 14-day dynamical prediction.
details:
Our project, Sea Level Detective, investigates how ocean and climate data can be used to predict coastal water levels in advance, using New York Harbor and the Los Angeles region as primary examples. We combine two complementary approaches: data-driven seasonal prediction and physics-based short-range ocean forecasting.

For seasonal prediction, we use NASA and NOAA datasets including satellite sea-surface-height observations, tide-gauge records, climate indices, winds and atmospheric pressure. We first separate the useful water-level signal from tides, long-term trends and seasonal cycles. Least-squares regression with Fourier terms represents annual and semiannual variability, while autocorrelation is taken into account so that statistical significance is not overstated. We then screen many possible predictors and test them on winters that were not used to select the model. One important result is that tropical-Pacific El Niño conditions, measured months before winter, provide useful information about subsequent high-water risk on both U.S. coasts. This demonstrates that remote ocean conditions can add predictive information beyond the local water-level history alone.

For shorter-range prediction, we use NASA sea-surface-height anomaly data together with NASA GEOS-FP atmospheric winds and OSCAR surface-current analyses. We developed a nonlinear shallow-water dynamical model that evolves departures from the observed ocean state and predicts changes over 7–14 days. Rather than merely fitting past water levels, this model uses physical processes including pressure-gradient forces, Coriolis effects, nonlinear advection, wind forcing, damping and diffusion. We evaluate forecasts chronologically against a strong persistence benchmark. On an extended 2023–2026 dataset, the 14-day hybrid physics forecast reduces sea-surface-height error by about 12% relative to persistence, with approximately 92% of forecasts outperforming persistence.

A key challenge is that sea-surface height changes slowly, making persistence—predicting no change—a strong benchmark. We therefore tune physically meaningful parameters such as effective wave speed/depth, damping, and the number of recent observations used to define the background state. Because the raw PDE tends to overestimate the magnitude of change, its predicted correction is scaled before being added to the latest observation. A hybrid forecast also adds a term proportional to the most recent weekly change, capturing short-term observed tendency.

Forecasts are evaluated chronologically. On the extended 2023–2026 dataset, the 14-day hybrid forecast reduces sea-surface-height error by about 12% relative to persistence, with approximately 92% of forecasts outperforming it.

The intended impact is to provide coastal communities with information on two useful timescales: months of advance warning for seasonal risk and fine-grained dynamical forecasts over the following two weeks. Such information can support emergency managers, ports, transit systems and coastal infrastructure operators in planning barriers, pumps, staffing and other preparedness measures.

The project was developed primarily in Python, using tools including NumPy, pandas, xarray, SciPy, Matplotlib, NetCDF and NASA Earthdata access tools. Data processing and numerical experiments were run on Linux workstations, with Git and GitHub used for collaborative development and reproducibility.

The project is creative in combining statistical learning, global Earth observations and mechanistic ocean physics in one forecasting framework. We considered seasonality, tides, long-term trends, autocorrelation, false discoveries, forecast-data leakage, persistence, spatial scale, atmospheric forcing, ocean-current structure and strict out-of-sample validation. Rather than relying on a single black-box predictor, the project asks both what remote observations provide predictive information and whether physical ocean dynamics can turn that information into improved forecasts.
